value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Redraw the image as a grid of text characters.

textSize: Size of one character cell in pixels.
cellAspect: Cell height as a multiple of its width. Above one gives tall cells, like real monospaced type.
margin: Padding inside each cell, as a fraction of it. Higher values space the characters further apart.
charset: Which glyph ramp to use. Classic is pixi.js's eight-level dot-to-hash ramp; Block Density, Dots, and Numeric are five, eight, and eleven steps native to this plugin; Letters and Full ASCII are twenty-six and ninety-five steps from the Tom Thumb font.
rampGamma: Bias of brightness onto the glyph ramp. Below one favours dense glyphs, above one sparse.
rampContrast: Pushes cells toward the sparsest and densest ends of the character set. A character set is a short ladder - Classic has eight rungs - so midtones crowd into the middle of it and the extreme glyphs hardly get used. This spends the whole set, which is the punchy posterised look that reads as ASCII art. Ramp Gamma cannot do it: gamma moves the midpoint but leaves both ends pinned.
structure: Picks the glyph whose SHAPE matches the cell rather than just its brightness, so an edge becomes a slash or a bar running the same way. Only available for Letters and Full ASCII: the other sets are density ramps of symmetric marks - Classic's eight glyphs are all but one symmetric - so there is no directional glyph for this to find and it correctly does nothing. Candidates stay near the density the cell already has, so tone survives; higher widens that search.
edgeThreshold: Above zero, cells on a boundary use a line glyph chosen by edge direction. This is the threshold the edge must clear.
colorMode: Colour from the layer, one flat colour with transparency between glyphs, or ink on a filled paper.
inkColor: Character colour, used by Single Colour and Ink On Paper.
paperColor: Background colour, used by Ink On Paper.
paletteLevels: Quantises each cell's colour to this many steps per channel. Zero is off.
invert: Flip the brightness ramp, so dark areas get the dense characters.
randomChars: Chance of a cell using a random glyph instead of its brightness one, for a scattered letterform look.
seed: Changes which cells are scattered and which characters they get.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the character result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Encode and decode the image as an analogue TV signal.

system: Broadcast standard. PAL gives a finer, slower dot pattern and steadier hues than NTSC; PAL-M is PAL colour on 525 lines.
time: Drives the animated interference and the subcarrier drift. Connected to comp time by default.
speed: How fast the interference and subcarrier move. Zero freezes the signal.
virtualRes: Line and sample grid the signal is quantised to. Keep the line count well below the layer's pixel height or it aliases.
saturation: Gain on both chroma axes after decoding.
blur: How much of the filtered luma replaces the raw luma. This is a transmission filter, so it rings rather than softens.
bandwidth: Passband of the decoder's luma and chroma filters, the real parameter that sets how much detail survives the signal path and how far colour bleeds sideways. Below 1 narrows both and softens the picture; above 1 opens them up and lets more subcarrier through as dot crawl.
peaking: Aperture correction - the mid-frequency boost a receiver applied to claw back the sharpness the camera and the tube's spot size had cost. This is where the crunchy, edgy look comes from; at 0 the picture is correctly filtered and noticeably softer.
blurSize: Spacing of the luma filter's taps. Wider spacing means a lower bandwidth and heavier ringing.
chromaBlur: How much of the filtered chroma replaces the raw chroma. Colour bleeding across edges comes from here.
chromaSize: Spacing of the chroma filter's taps. Composite colour bandwidth is far below luma's, so this is normally much wider.
qNarrow: NTSC only: how much harder the Q axis is filtered than I, which is what makes colour bleed directional.
subcarrier: Strength of the colour subcarrier left visible in the picture - the fine dot crawl over saturated areas.
phaseError: Differential phase - how far the subcarrier's phase drifts at peak white on its way down the transmission path. This is the defect the three systems differ over: NTSC passes it through as a brightness-dependent hue shift, while PAL's line-alternating V cancels it into a small loss of saturation.
crosstalk: How much of the subcarrier leaks into luma, so colour makes the picture shimmer.
crossColour: Fine luma detail leaking into the colour decoder - the rainbow on herringbone and fine stripes.
hanover: PAL only: weakens the delay line, giving fine banding in line pairs. Worst on saturated flats.
scanlines: Depth of the line structure. Zero is off, which is also what you want when checking that the signal path returns the original colours.
scanFlicker: Vertical jitter alternating frame to frame, standing in for interlace.
interference2: Occasional strong disturbance that smears and brightens a band of lines.
fishEye: Horizontal and vertical curvature of the screen.
tubeOverscan: How far the raster is drawn past the faceplate. A real set overscans so the picture runs off the glass rather than showing an unpainted border where the tube's bulge pulled the edges in.
vignetteRounding: Shape of the tube mask. High values give squarer corners.
vignetteSmoothness: Softness of the tube mask's edge. Very small values make the mask disappear.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the broadcast result.
vRoll: Speed the picture rolls at when vertical sync is lost. Signed - positive and negative roll opposite ways. Zero holds the picture still.
vRollJump: How much the roll stutters in discrete line jumps rather than sliding smoothly.
hTear: How far affected scanlines jump sideways when horizontal sync briefly fails.
hTearDensity: Fraction of lines torn on any given frame. Higher values tear more lines at once, in short bursts.
ghostAmount: Strength of a second, delayed copy of the picture, as from a reflected aerial signal.
ghostDelay: How far to the right the ghost trails behind the main picture.
snow: Amount of white noise speckle, strongest where the picture is darkest.
snowBurst: How much the snow clumps into intermittent bursts rather than a constant speckle.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Screen emulation: CRT shadow masks, LCD stripe, curvature and beam.

distortion: Barrel curvature of the glass. The tube outline and corners bow with it.
overscan: How far the raster is drawn past the faceplate, as a real set does so the picture runs off the glass rather than showing an unpainted border. 1 fills the tube exactly at any distortion; below 1 the bowed raster edge becomes visible.
edges: What to do where the curvature samples outside the layer. Transparent is honest - there is no picture there. Clamp smears the rim outward, Mirror reflects the picture back.
edgeTrim: Pixels to inset the edge that Clamp and Mirror fold against, so they reflect real picture rather than the layer's antialiased rim.
cornerRadius: Radius of the rounded tube corners, in pixels. Clamped to half the short side.
borderSoftness: How many pixels the faceplate edge feathers over. Zero is the pixel-sharp edge; a real faceplate is not sharp, since the glass has thickness and the mask behind it is not perfectly registered to it.
vignette: Brightness falloff toward the corners, following the cos⁴ law - the real reason a lens darkens off-axis, rather than a drawn curve.
mask: Sub-pixel structure. Shadow Mask, Aperture Grille and Slot Mask are hex-packed, wire and slot phosphor geometries; LCD Stripe is an aligned RGB stripe.
pixelSize: Size of one addressable pixel, in screen pixels. The same square cell for every mask, so switching Mask does not change the scale.
pixelate: How much the picture is quantised to the pixel grid.
maskAmount: Strength of the sub-pixel mask against the unmasked picture.
gridGap: Darkness of the black grid line between LCD cells.
stagger: Offsets alternate columns. Zero reads as a flat panel; one gives the staggered CRT look.
dotSize: Size of the dot, wire or slot within its cell, for Shadow Mask, Aperture Grille and Slot Mask.
maskSaturation: How coloured the phosphors are. At 1 they are full red, green and blue; at 0 they are neutral grey dots with black between them. Turn this down rather than Mask Amount when the texture is right but the colour is loud.
maskSoftness: How soft the phosphor edges are. 1 is about one screen pixel, which is what stops the mask aliasing; raise it to diffuse the dots, drop it toward 0 for a hard-edged digital look.
scanlines: Depth of the dark gap between the lines the tube draws. One line per virtual pixel row.
scanlineThickness: Fraction of each line's pitch that is lit. Lower is a thinner, harder line.
gain: Exposure after the mask. A mask that passes one channel per pixel has to be boosted to hold its brightness, and that boost clips the dots to white, so a strong mask always costs some light. Raise this to win it back.
beamAmount: Strength of the scanning-beam effect. Zero leaves the picture unchanged.
beamHeight: How tall the brightly-illuminated band is, as a fraction of one full sweep.
beamSpeed: Rolling rate of the beam: sweeps of the frame per unit of Time.
beamDecay: Phosphor persistence trailing the beam. Higher lingers longer after the beam passes.
beamPhase: Manual offset of the beam's position within its sweep.
aberration: Chromatic aberration, increasing toward the edges.
bloom: Weighted glow spreading light off bright areas.
bloomRadius: How far Bloom and Diffusion reach, in pixels. Both share this gather, so it needs to cross a mask cell before either can soften the dots.
diffusion: Light scattering in the glass face. Unlike Bloom it lifts everything, not just highlights, so blacks wash toward grey the way a real tube's do.
time: Drives the grain and the beam sweep. Connected to comp time by default.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the screen result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Key out a range of a channel, with feathered edges.

channel: Which value the key is based on. Luminance is the usual choice; Red, Green, Blue and Alpha key off a single channel of the layer instead.
blackSoftness: Feathers the transition at the Black Point instead of a hard cutoff.
whiteSoftness: Feathers the transition at the White Point instead of a hard cutoff.
invert: Swaps kept for removed - the range between the two points becomes transparent instead of opaque.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Film stock: halation, tone roll-off, grain and a colour recipe.

halation: Warm bloom from light scattering back through the film base, spreading around highlights.
halationRadius: How far the halation spreads, in pixels. The layer bounds expand to match.
halationThreshold: Luminance above which highlights start to glow. Softly thresholded, so the matte has no hard edge.
halationDensity: How much denser the core of the glow is than its falloff. Higher makes only the brightest highlights bloom.
halationRing: Hollows the core so the halation stands off the highlight as a fringe rather than glowing from its centre. This is what halation physically is - light that crosses the emulsion, bounces off the base and re-exposes it a fixed distance away, set by the thickness of the base. At 0 you get a plain glow.
halationTint: Which channels the scatter shows up in. The original used a deep orange, so it lands mostly in red.
linearise: Applies a 2.2 transfer before the tone curve and undoes it after. Off by default - Cavalry has its own colour management.
exposure: Stops of gain before the tone curve. This is what drives highlights into the roll-off.
rolloff: Compresses highlights through a filmic shoulder. It needs something above white to compress, so raise Exposure or Halation first - on a plain 0-1 image it has nothing to work on and only lifts the midtones.
gamutExtension: Width of the gamut the roll-off happens inside. Wider desaturates highlights further before they clip.
recipe: Strength of the Recipe tab's Fujifilm-style grade. 0 leaves colour untouched.
base: Starting colour character, built from published descriptions of a film simulation. Mono and Mono Flat are black and white.
colour: Overall saturation trim, on Fujifilm's -4 to +4 scale.
highlightTone: Density of the highlights, -2 to +4. Positive is harder, negative softer.
shadowTone: Density of the shadows, -2 to +4. Positive crushes them, negative opens them up.
highlightProtect: Highlight protection, as the camera's DR100 / DR200 / DR400. Higher holds the top end back.
colourChrome: Deepens colours that are already saturated, leaving pale ones alone. Off, Weak (0.5) or Strong (1.0).
colourChromeBlue: The same, restricted to blues and cyans - for skies and deep blues specifically.
wbShiftR: Red trim on Fujifilm's white balance shift grid, -9 to +9.
wbShiftB: Blue trim on the same grid. Positive is cooler, negative warmer.
monoToning: Warm or cool cast for the black and white bases, matching MonochromaticColor. No effect on the colour bases.
clarity: Local contrast, -5 to +5: micro-contrast without touching overall tone. Negative softens the way a diffusion filter does.
clarityRadius: Size of the detail Clarity acts on, in pixels. Small values sharpen fine texture, large values shape broad areas.
grain: Film grain strength (k in the signal-dependent model x + k*x^gamma*u).
grainSize: Feature size of the grain in pixels. Coarser grain is also stronger, as it is on real stock - a bigger crystal is a bigger fluctuation under the same sampling aperture.
grainBlur: How sharply each grain is defined. Low gives soft, diffuse crystals; high gives hard-edged ones you can pick out individually. Grains are round discs at random positions, so this never introduces a grid however large Grain Size goes.
grainResponse: How tightly grain concentrates in the midtones. Real film is grainiest where the emulsion is half developed and cleans up in both the highlights and the deep shadows - 1 is that physical curve. Below 1 spreads grain toward the extremes, above 1 confines it further to the midtones.
grainDomain: Whether grain is added before or after the tone curve. Positive Print grains the developed image; Negative grains before it, so the curve reshapes the grain too.
scannerNoise: Separate white noise modelling a telecine/scanner's own sensor noise, independent of film grain.
time: Driven by the composition time. Disconnect it to freeze the film artefacts.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the film result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Burn a hole through the layer, as film stalling in the gate.

progress: How far the burn has eaten through. 0 is untouched, 1 is fully gone.
origin: Where the hole first appears: the frame centre, an edge, a corner, or a point you place yourself.
position: Where the hole starts, offset from the layer centre in pixels. Only used when Starts From is set to Manual.
scale: Feature size of the noise that ravels the edge, in pixels. Larger values give broad, lazy tears; smaller values give fine, busy ones.
roughness: How much the noise warps the edge away from a plain circle or front. Zero burns in a clean shape; higher values make it ragged and organic.
seed: Shifts the noise pattern without changing its character, so different instances of the filter burn through differently.
charWidth: Width of the blackened ring right at the edge of the hole, in field units.
charColor: Colour of the charred film immediately around the hole.
burnWidth: Width of the bright ring where the film is actively alight.
burnColor: Colour of the active burn front.
bloomWidth: Width of the pre-ignition glow ahead of the burn front, where the emulsion is heating but hasn't caught yet.
bloomIntensity: How far the bloom blows out toward white before it settles into the untouched picture.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the burnt result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Print wear: gate weave, dirt, scratches, flicker and vignette.

damage: Strength of the Damage tab's projector wear. 0 is a pristine print.
damageDomain: Whether dirt, scratches, vignette and flicker are applied to the print or to the (inverted) negative, which changes how they land in highlights versus shadows.
time: Driven by the composition time. Disconnect it to freeze the film artefacts.
timeOffset: Frames to subtract before the projector's clock starts. A filter cannot see its layer's in point - it only gets comp time - so set this to the in point (an expression works) and the wear begins when the layer does. Without it every layer in a comp shows the same weave, flicker and dirt at the same instant, which is the giveaway that one filter has been applied many times. Offsetting moves the whole projector together, so nothing drifts out of step.
speed: How fast the damage clock runs relative to real time. 1 is real time; lower slows the judder and weave, higher speeds them up.
frameRate: Steps time to this rate for a projected-film judder. Zero leaves motion smooth.
weave: How much the picture wanders in the gate, as a fraction of the layer. A mean-reverting wander rather than a steady drift.
dirtThreshold: How many specks land, as the chance of a particle per cell. Sizes follow a power law from there - mostly tiny, with the occasional large flake - so this changes how much dirt there is, not how big it is.
dirtScale: Base size of the specks. Individual particles vary widely around this, since real dust does.
dirtBurst: How much the amount of dirt varies from frame to frame. At 0 every frame carries the same density, which is the giveaway that it is generated - real prints have clean stretches and filthy ones, because dust arrives in clumps and a dirty section stays dirty for a while. Bursts last about three frames, and clean frames are the norm.
dirtSoftness: How far off the focal plane the dust sits. Zero is dust at the film plane, as sharp as the picture itself; higher is dust on the gate glass or on the negative a generation back, which prints soft. Particles keep their size either way - only the edge loses its bite.
dirtPolarity: Which generation the dust landed on. Negative is dirt on the print or in the gate: it blocks light and reads black. Positive is dirt on the NEGATIVE, which blocks exposure so the print stays clear there and projects as bright white sparkle - the classic archive-print artefact. Zero gives both.
scratches: Density of vertical gate scratches - thin, flickering, drifting sideways over time.
scratchWidth: Base width of a scratch in pixels. Real scratches are thin - keep this small.
flicker: Frame-to-frame exposure wobble, log-normal like a real lamp/shutter flicker rather than symmetric.
gateRounding: Shape of the projector gate the light falls off through. 1 is a true ellipse; lower values square the corners toward the rectangular aperture a real gate has. A superellipse, so there is no curvature break where the corners meet the sides.
gateSoftness: How far the gate edge feathers. Small is a hard-edged mask; large is the gentle falloff of an old projector lens.
vignetteFlicker: How much the vignette breathes over time.
desaturate: One is full black and white, as in the original. Lower it to keep some colour.
surroundGamma: The extra contrast a print carries because it is meant to be seen in a blacked-out room. A dark surround makes the eye perceive less contrast, so prints are made with a system gamma around 1.2 to compensate - which is why projected film looks punchier than the same footage on a monitor. 1 switches it off.
dyeFade: Cyan is the least stable of the three print dyes and fades first, then magenta, with yellow the most durable. Losing cyan means less red gets absorbed, which is why old prints drift magenta-red rather than simply going grey.
hotSpot: Projector lamps are brighter on the optical axis. The opposite gradient to the gate vignette, and not cancelled by it.
scratchPolarity: Which side of the film is scratched. Negative is the base - the shiny side - where scratches read dark. Positive is the emulsion, where the gouge takes the dyes away and reads bright. Zero gives both.
shutterBlades: Blade count of the projector shutter, 2 or 3 on a real machine. The blades chop the light faster than the frame rate, so they cannot show as flicker in a rendered frame - what you get here is the beat against the frame rate, which is what a camera pointed at a screen records. 0 switches it off.
splice: Strength of the jolt as a physical join passes the gate: the print jumps vertically and the density pops for a frame or two.
spliceInterval: Seconds between joins. Prints are assembled from a few hundred feet at a time.
cueMarks: The reel-changeover cue punched into the top-right corner - the “cigarette burn” that tells the projectionist to start the second machine.
cueInterval: Seconds between cues. A real reel runs about 20 minutes. 0 pins the mark on permanently, for when you want the mark rather than the schedule.
hair: A hair caught in the gate, trembling as the film drags past but otherwise fixed. Use Hair Seed to reposition it.
hairSeed: Which hair you get and where it sits. It stays put - a hair in the gate holds its position until someone cleans the machine - so change this to move it rather than expecting it to wander.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the film result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Bloom and anamorphic streaks from the image's own highlights.

srcBlack: Only light above this emits. This is the black point of the grade that isolates the highlights.
srcWhite: Level that counts as fully lit. Below 1 pushes more of the picture into the glow.
response: Curve of the highlight grade. Higher keeps the glow tight around genuinely bright areas.
streakAmount: Strength of the directional smear. Zero leaves a pure bloom.
streakIntensity: Brightness of the streak on top of the global Intensity, so the flare can be pushed or pulled against the bloom rather than both moving together.
reach: Total streak length in pixels. The layer bounds expand to match.
angle: Streak axis in degrees. Zero is the classic horizontal anamorphic bar.
samples: How densely each pass samples along the streak. This sets quality only - the streak is the same length at any setting - and 4 is the minimum at which the passes still tile without gaps.
streakFalloff: How quickly the streak fades along its length. The profile is the envelope of a diffraction spike - it falls off as one over distance squared, so the streak keeps a faint tail right across the frame the way a real one does, rather than stopping abruptly.
blur: How far the streak is softened ACROSS its width, as a true gaussian in its own pass. Earlier versions borrowed the streak's own samples for this, which could only ever produce copies or noise rather than a blur.
bidirectional: Smear both ways for a symmetric bar. Off gives a comet trail.
chromatic: Splits the streak into seven spectral bands, so it fringes warm one way and cool the other.
dispersion: How far the colour bands separate, in pixels. Negative swaps which end is warm.
bloomAmount: Strength of the isotropic glow. Zero leaves a pure streak.
haloAmount: A coloured ring standing at a fixed distance from each highlight - the halo you see around a streetlight at night. Not a falloff like Bloom: diffraction off the radial fibres in the eye's lens throws light out to one particular radius, and because the angle scales with wavelength the ring is chromatic on its own, red outside and blue in.
haloRadius: How far out the ring sits, in pixels. Red lands about 13% further than green and blue about 18% closer, which is what colours it.
haloSoftness: Width of the ring. Thin gives a sharp chromatic band; wide gives a soft halo whose red and blue edges blend through each other.
size: Widest radius in the bloom ladder, in pixels.
falloff: Scales the whole ladder. Above one pulls the bloom in tighter.
steps: How many rungs of the bloom ladder to run. Each rung is twice the width of the last, so more steps means a wider, softer veil for more cost; fewer means a tighter glow that renders faster. This used to divide the result without changing how many rungs ran, so low values simply overexposed.
persistence: Gains the wide end of the ladder, for a longer, softer tail.
intensity: Glow brightness. A wide glow spreads a highlight's energy far, so expect to push this up.
saturation: Colour of the veil, separate from the picture and from the halo. Scattered light is close to achromatic - the standard glare models treat the veiling term as having no colour at all, and only the halo as wavelength-dependent - so a bright red lamp throws a whitish veil. Above 1 for when the colour is the point.
blend: How the glow combines with the layer. Effect Only shows the glow alone.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Volumetric light shafts from turbulence in ray-space.

angle: Direction the rays travel in, in degrees. Zero is vertical.
parallel: On for rays travelling in one direction (Angle). Off for rays radiating from a point (Light).
light: Offset of the ray source from the layer centre, in pixels. Radiating rays only.
rayMode: Which model builds the shafts. Volumetric samples Perlin turbulence along the ray direction - soft, cloudy, atmospheric, and the more physical of the two. Light Field samples value noise in polar space and multiplies two sparse fields together, which gives crisper, separated shafts with hard edges. Light Field is also several times cheaper: two noise evaluations against eighteen.
gain: Strength of the turbulence that shapes the shafts. Zero is a passthrough.
lacunarity: Frequency step between turbulence octaves. Higher breaks the shafts into finer, busier detail.
density: How tightly packed the shafts are.
speed: How fast the shafts drift. 0 holds them still.
scatterG: How strongly the haze throws light FORWARD. Scattering off dust and droplets is forward-peaked, so shafts blaze when you look near the light and fade as you turn away - which is most of what makes crepuscular rays read as light rather than as texture. 0 scatters equally in all directions; 0.7 to 0.9 is real atmospheric haze.
blur: Softens the shafts across their width. It works on the ray pattern, not the picture.
spotty: How quickly a shaft loses coherence along its length. Low keeps rays long and continuous; high breaks them into short spots, because the second noise field advances faster with distance and decorrelates from the first.
rayIntensity: Crushes everything but the peaks of the noise, so the shafts narrow and separate. This is the one control doing the work that extra noise octaves would otherwise do.
rayCount: Roughly how many shafts fan out around the light. This is the Light Field model's angular frequency; Density is the Volumetric model's noise scale and means something different, which is why they are two controls rather than one.
spread: Angular extent of the cone, centred on Angle. At 1 the rays go all the way round the light; lower confines them to a wedge. Radiating rays only - parallel rays have no origin to fan out from.
coreSize: Radius of the glow sitting at the light itself.
coreGlow: Brightness of that glow. It is not only additive: it also multiplies the rays near it, up to five times, so shafts blaze where they leave the source instead of merely crossing a bright blob.
rayColor: Colour of the shafts. White leaves them uncoloured, which is what earlier versions did unconditionally.
rayColor2: A second colour, interleaved shaft by shaft along the angular coordinate rather than by brightness - so neighbouring shafts differ and the fan reads as dispersed light. Set it to match Ray Colour for a single tint.
time: Driven by the composition time. Disconnect it to freeze the shafts.
amount: Amount
Overall opacity of the ray effect over the original layer.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Redraw the image as pen strokes, dots or halftone cells.

pattern: Which mark to draw. The first three are threshold-layered; the rest are continuous-width lines.
size: Line period, or cell size for Cross Stitch, in pixels.
lineWidth: Thickness of the marks. Interacts with Size: the ratio of the two sets how solid dark areas go.
angle: Direction of the marks, in degrees. Used by Lines and by the two dot screens, where it sets the screen angle; the other patterns have no single direction to rotate.
softness: Edge softness of the mark. On the dot screens this is also what makes neighbouring dots run together into blobs as the image darkens, rather than staying separate discs.
threshold1: Crosshatch only. Luminance below which the first family appears. Luminance here is length(RGB), so the range is 0 to 1.74.
threshold2: Crosshatch only. Luminance below which the second, crossing family appears.
threshold3: Crosshatch only. Luminance below which the third family appears.
threshold4: Crosshatch only. The darkest areas get all four families.
offset: Crosshatch only. Shifts the third and fourth families so they do not sit on top of the first two.
warpAmount: Currency only. How far the lines wander, as a fraction of the layer height.
warpFrequency: Currency only. Wave cycles across the layer height.
layers: Currency only. How many of the six line families to draw. Fewer gives a sparser pattern.
brightness: Cross Stitch only. Gain on the thread colour; the original used 1.4 to stop stitches reading too dark.
invert: Cross Stitch only. Swap thread and background, so stitches become solid ink and the gaps carry the image.
inkColor: Colour of the mark. Cross Stitch takes its thread colour from the image instead, unless Invert Stitch is on.
transparentPaper: Output the mark and its alpha only, with no background, so it composites straight over whatever sits behind the layer.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the hatched result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Redraw the image as a matrix of LED lamps.

cellSize: Grid pitch in pixels - the spacing between lamps.
stagger: Offsets alternate rows. Zero is a square grid, one is a fully offset hex grid.
dotSize: Lamp diameter as a fraction of the cell. Above one the lamps touch and merge.
roundness: Zero is a square lamp, one is a circle.
softness: Edge falloff in pixels. Raise it for a glowing lamp, drop it for a hard pixel.
sizeFromBrightness: Drives lamp radius from image brightness, so dark areas get small lamps. This is the behaviour of the original lightbulb shader.
perChannel: Drive each colour's lamp separately rather than one lamp tinted by the pixel.
bgColor: Colour filling the gaps between lamps.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the LED result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Lens geometry: barrel distortion and chromatic aberration.

profile: Which measured HAWK anamorphic focal length to apply, solved from a real distortion chart.
distortion: Scales the chosen profile's strength. 1.0 reproduces the solved lens; use this to match a plate rather than as a cosmetic dial.
squeeze: Anamorphic squeeze ratio. Stretches the frame horizontally as a taking lens does.
centreOffset: Shifts the optical centre, as a fraction of half the layer height. The HAWK profiles carry no baked-in centre of their own.
expand: Scales the sampled area. Raise it slightly to pull the distorted edges back inside the frame.
edges: What to do where the distortion samples outside the layer. Transparent is honest - there is no picture there. Clamp smears the rim outward, Mirror reflects the picture back; both fill the wedges a barrel distortion opens at the corners.
edgeTrim: Pixels to inset the edge that Clamp and Mirror fold against. A layer's outermost pixels are antialiased, so reflecting them doubles the rim into a seam; a pixel or two of trim folds against real picture instead.
fringing: Chromatic spread across the distortion, so the fringe follows the glass. This replaces the old Barrel model, which was this pass with a spectrum.
abModel: Which aberration to apply. None switches this half of the lens off.
geometry: Direction the bands separate: radially from the centre, spun around it, or along a fixed angle.
centre: Origin for radial and spin geometry, in pixels from the layer centre.
angle: Direction for linear geometry, and for Prism when its direction is not taken from the map.
dispersion: Spectral and Prism. Magnitude of the separation between wavelength bands.
focusWave: Spectral and Prism. Which wavelength stays sharp: -1 violet, 0 green, 1 red. Everything either side separates.
smoothing: Spectral only. Widens each band to bridge the gaps between the seven, melting them together.
aberration: Channel only. Displacement in pixels before the per-channel scales.
redScale: Channel only. Multiplier on red's displacement.
greenScale: Channel only. Multiplier on green's displacement.
blueScale: Channel only. Multiplier on blue's displacement.
smear: Smears each channel along its displacement instead of just offsetting it. Channel model only.
falloff: Channel only. How quickly radial displacement grows outward. Higher keeps the centre cleaner.
mapChannel: Prism only. Which part of the displacement map drives the effect.
mapAmplitude: Prism only. Displacement in pixels at the map's full value.
mapFromGradient: Take the displacement direction from the map's own slope rather than from the Angle control.
abIntensity: Spectral and Prism. Overall brightness of the result.
samples: Tap count, shared by fringing and the spectral aberration.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the full lens.
displaceMap: Prism only. The shader whose luminance drives the displacement. Prism does nothing until something is connected here.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Defocus with a real diaphragm shape, plus lens scatter.

bokehThreshold: How bright a pixel must be to count as a highlight and be weighted up by Gain. Below this nothing is changed, so raising it narrows the bokeh to the brightest points only.
bokehGamma: How hard highlights outweigh everything else in the blur. This is what turns a bright point into a defined disc rather than a soft smear: the picture is raised to this power before blurring and taken back afterwards, so a flat area returns exactly as it was and only the bright points spread. Higher is more defined; around 4 is a good starting point.
defocus: Blur radius in pixels. Zero switches the blur off. A non-uniform Focus From can scale this up to 4x, which the layer padding does not account for - pull Blur back if you see clipping.
blades: Aperture shape. Round is a lens near wide open, where the diaphragm blades retract clear of the light path and the aperture is the barrel itself. The blade counts are a stopped-down lens, where the blades are in the way and the highlight takes their polygon.
rotation: Turns the whole aperture, in degrees.
bokehSqueeze: 1 is spherical - out-of-focus highlights come out round. Anything else squeezes them into ellipses, the way an anamorphic lens does. This is the strongest single cue that footage came through one.
bokehAngle: The axis the squeeze acts along, so the ellipses can tilt rather than sitting square to frame.
catsEye: Optical vignetting. Clips the aperture toward the frame edge, so highlights out there turn into lemons pointing at the centre.
catsEyeFalloff: How quickly the clipping grows away from the centre. Higher keeps the middle of frame round for longer.
ringBias: Where the light sits inside the out-of-focus disc. Positive brightens the rim - ring, or soap-bubble bokeh, from a lens under-corrected for spherical aberration. Negative brightens the centre, the soft creamy rendering portrait lenses are prized for. Zero is a flat disc.
cocSource: What decides how blurred each pixel is. Uniform blurs everything equally. Focus Region keeps an area of the frame sharp and is by far the cheapest. Map reads the shader in the Map tab - accurate, but every sample re-evaluates that shader, so a heavy graph is slow. Luminance and Alpha use the layer's own matte.
mapMode: How the map in this tab is interpreted. Brightness takes it literally - white blurs, black stays sharp - which is what a hand-painted blur map wants. Depth treats it as distance, so the blur is worked out around Focus and rises on BOTH sides of it, leaving a sharp band that Focus slides through. That is what a rendered depth pass wants.
focus: The value in the matte that stays sharp; anything further from it blurs more. Used by Alpha, Luminance and Depth Map - Focus Region places the sharp area in the frame instead.
aperture: How fast the blur grows away from the focal plane. The falloff is the thin-lens hyperbola, so something a step nearer than focus blurs harder than something the same step further away, as a real lens does.
focusShape: Circle is a focus vignette - sharp inside the size, blurring outward. Line is a sharp band running across the frame, which is the tilt-shift look.
focusPoint: Where the sharp region sits, as an offset from the layer centre. Push it off-frame with a Line to get a plain gradient from sharp to blurred.
focusSize: Radius of the sharp circle, or half the width of the sharp band.
focusAspect: Stretches the sharp circle into an ellipse - a wide sharp zone across a landscape, or a tall one down a portrait. 1 is round. Focus Angle turns it.
focusSoftness: How many pixels the blur takes to come on past the focus region. Small values give a hard edge to the blur, which no lens does; large values are the gentle falloff of a real focal plane.
focusAngle: Turns the Line band, or the Focus Aspect ellipse.
exposure: Rolls the discs off rather than letting them clip. Gain multiplies before the blur, so pushed hard it flattens highlights to solid white; this is a compressive curve applied after, which lifts them but never reaches 1, so they keep their falloff. Use Gain for how much a disc dominates, this for how it behaves near white.
gain: How much extra weight highlights carry INTO the blur, so it sets how strongly the discs dominate the background rather than just how bright they are. A plain multiply, so it will clip - Highlight Exposure is there to roll that off.
dither: Jitters tap positions to trade banding along the aperture edges for fine grain.
occlusion: Stops a blurred background smearing over a sharp foreground: a point of light only spreads as far as its own circle of confusion, so a sharp pixel cannot reach a distant one. Needs real depth to mean anything, and it is the expensive control - it re-reads the map once per sample, roughly 96 times a pixel. Off unless you can see the bleed.
edges: What the blur does where it reaches outside the layer. Transparent is honest - there is no picture there - but it drags a dark rim inward at large radii. Clamp smears the rim outward, Mirror reflects the picture back.
edgeTrim: Pixels to inset the edge that Clamp and Mirror fold against. A layer's outermost pixels are antialiased, so reflecting them doubles the rim into a seam.
kernel: The shape light scatters into. Disc is spherical aberration, Line is astigmatism, Rings is diffraction, Halo is haze.
size: Radius of the artefact scatter, in pixels. Zero switches the artefacts off.
ringFrequency: How many diffraction rings fit inside the radius. Only used by the Rings kernel.
axialRed: Kernel size multiplier for red. Setting the three channels apart gives axial chromatic aberration.
scatterThreshold: Only light above this level scatters. Lower it to let midtones haze as well.
scatterBlend: How the scatter combines with the layer. Replace shows the scatter alone.
samples: Tap count for the artefact scatter. The blur's own tap count is fixed by its segment passes.
amount: Amount
Mixes the whole filter back against the untouched layer.
defocusMap: The shader this filter reads for focus. A rendered depth pass through Shape to Shader, an image through Image Shader, or any shader node. Read As decides whether it means blur or distance.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Ghosts, halo and starburst from the image's highlights.

placement: How the emitter position is found. Auto tracks the brightest region in the frame; Manual lets you place it anywhere, including off screen.
position: Emitter offset from the layer centre, in pixels. Works fine outside the frame bounds - that is the usual case for a real flare.
colourSource: Where the flare's colour comes from. From Image takes it from the highlight the flare sits on; Manual lets you set it outright.
brightnessSource: Where the flare's strength comes from. From Image fades it with the highlight underneath; Manual renders it at full strength wherever you place it.
flareColour: The flare's colour in Manual mode. Brightness still comes from the image, so the flare keeps responding to how blown out the highlight is.
threshold: Only light above this feeds the flare. This is the black point of the grade that isolates the highlights.
gamma: Curve of the highlight grade. Higher keeps every element tight around genuinely bright areas.
lens: Which lens's surfaces the ghost pattern is traced from. Fast Prime and Standard Zoom are paraxially traced from real optical-bench prescriptions; Anamorphic is a derived approximation and squeezes every ghost horizontally.
ghostIntensity: Strength of the reflection ghosts. Zero removes them entirely.
ghostSoft: How defocused the ghosts are. A ghost forms at the wrong focal distance, so it is genuinely out of focus - at 0 you get hard-edged polygons, which is the main thing that makes a flare look drawn.
ghostCount: How many ghosts to draw, out of a fixed maximum of 8, revealed in order of how bright that reflection path actually is on the chosen lens.
ghostSpacing: Scales how far each ghost sits from frame centre. Each ghost has its own baked distance and direction from the lens trace, so raising this spreads an already-irregular pattern rather than fixing its rhythm.
ghostScale: Overall ghost size. Each ghost keeps its own baked size relative to the others.
ghostChromatic: Strength of each ghost's own dispersion. The direction and amount differ per ghost, baked from how that reflection path shifts with wavelength - not one fringe applied to all of them.
ghostCatsEye: Optical vignetting on the ghosts. Clips each one toward frame centre from its own position, so ghosts that land off-axis turn into lemons instead of staying round.
ghostCatsEyeFalloff: How quickly that clipping grows with a ghost's distance from centre. Higher keeps ghosts near the middle round for longer.
blades: Aperture shape carved into each ghost and the starburst spikes. Zero is round. Matches the Lens filter's own Blades control, so a scene's flare and its bokeh agree on the diaphragm.
haloIntensity: Strength of the ring around the frame centre. Zero removes it entirely.
haloRadius: Distance from the frame centre to the ring, in pixels.
haloWidth: How wide the ring is, in pixels.
haloChromatic: Per-channel radius offset, in pixels, so the ring fringes.
haloBlur: Softens the halo across the ring. Without it the ring echoes the source's detail sharply, which an internal reflection never does.
starIntensity: Strength of the diffraction spikes at the emitter. Zero removes it entirely.
starLength: How far the spikes reach, in pixels.
starRotation: Spins the whole starburst, in degrees.
starSoftness: How crisp the diffraction spikes are. Above 1 the sinc's side ripples fade toward a plain glow; at 0 they are as sharp as the maths allows.
starGlow: Veiling glow around the core. The sharp centre is real - it is the diffraction pattern's central lobe - but a lens always scatters light around it too, and without that the spikes read as a drawn asterisk.
streakIntensity: Strength of the anamorphic bar through the emitter. Zero removes it entirely.
streakLength: How far the streak reaches from the emitter, in pixels.
streakAngle: Streak axis in degrees. Zero is horizontal.
intensity: Flare brightness. A wide flare spreads a highlight's energy far, so expect to push this up.
tint: Colour multiplier on the whole flare.
blend: How the flare combines with the layer. Effect Only shows the flare alone.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Stray light fogging in from an edge or corner.

intensity: Overall strength of the leak. Zero is an exact passthrough.
source: Where the light gets in: an edge, a corner, or a manual point.
position: Offset from the layer centre in pixels, used only when Source is Manual.
spread: How far the leak reaches in from its source before it fades away.
wander: How much the leak drifts in and out of frame over time. Above zero it recedes past the edge for stretches and comes back, so a shot is not lit by the same leak end to end. Speed sets how quickly it moves.
red: Strength of the red colour band.
yellow: Strength of the yellow colour band.
blue: Strength of the blue colour band.
interact: How much the leak is driven by the picture's own brightness, so it blooms in highlights and stays weak in shadow rather than sitting on top like a sticker.
speed: How fast the bands wobble and drift.
time: Driven by the composition time. Disconnect it to freeze the leak.
blend: How the leak combines with the picture: Screen and Lighten are the original's two modes, Add is a stronger third option.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Bleed a background layer's light in around this layer's edges.

size: How far light wraps in from the edge, in pixels.
falloff: Scales the whole blur ladder. Above one pulls the wrap tighter to the edge, below one spreads it further in.
aspect: Stretches the wrap horizontally against vertically.
useLuminance: Only let the brighter parts of the background wrap, rather than all of it.
threshold: How bright the background must be to wrap, when Bright Areas Only is on.
bgSize: Pixel resolution of the background image. Sets where it sits; without it the background reads as almost black.
bgScale: Corrects for the background being shown at a different size to its native resolution. 1.0 if shown at 100%.
gamma: Falloff curve of the wrap from the edge inward.
saturation: Colour strength of the wrapped light.
blend: How the wrap combines with the layer. Effect Only shows the wrap alone.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the wrapped result.
background: The background layer's shader. Nothing happens until this is connected.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Refraction through parallel ribs, as reeded or fluted glass.

ribWidth: Period of the ribs, in pixels.
angle: Direction of the ribs, in degrees.
shape: How the ribs run. The bend is added to the coordinate BEFORE it is wrapped, so a wave stays one continuous rib rather than breaking into steps.
profile: Cross-section of each rib, which is what sets the character of the refraction. Prism is a cubic sawtooth - hard, faceted. Lens is a parabola. Contour has a flat centre and steep shoulders. Cascade is a true arc. Flat is nearly linear with soft ends.
distortion: How far each rib bends the picture behind it.
shift: Biases the whole profile one way, so the ribs refract off-centre.
blur: Softens across the ribs, for etched rather than polished glass. Twelve jittered taps - a fixed ladder of taps stays a visible ladder however long it gets, so the jitter matters more than the count.
stretch: Pulls the sample toward each rib's centre line near its shoulders, smearing the picture there.
highlights: A thin stroke along each rib boundary. It is also the antialiasing: the stroke is two pixels wide, so when the ribs go sub-pixel it swallows them and the pattern greys out cleanly.
shadows: Darkening across each rib, from the profile's own curve.
edges: What a tap finds outside the layer. Transparent is the honest answer; Clamp and Mirror fill the wedge the refraction opens at the border.
edgeTrim: Fold against a rect inset by this much, so the antialiased outer pixels are not reflected into a seam.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Chrome, smoke or heat, shaped by the layer's own alpha.

material: Which shading head runs over the shape field. The field itself is built the same way for all three.
spread: How far the shape field reaches, in pixels. This is the falloff distance that upstream gets by normalising against the whole image - as a control it is better, because a thick stroke and a thin one on the same layer both read correctly instead of being scaled against each other.
contourAmount: How hard the field bends the material at the silhouette. Low leaves the pattern flat across the shape; high crowds it against the edges, which is what makes the surface look like it wraps the form.
repetition: How many light/dark bands the stripe field repeats. Think of it as how tightly banded the environment being reflected is.
softness: Edge softness of each band. Zero gives hard chrome; higher gives a brushed or satin surface.
shiftRed: Phase offset of the red channel against green. Together with Blue Shift this is the entire chromatic aberration - three samples of one field at three offsets, which is why the fringing follows the strokes and not the frame.
shiftBlue: Phase offset of the blue channel. Negative swaps which side of an edge goes warm.
distortion: Noise added into the field before it warps the bands, so the reflection ripples rather than sitting still. On Heat this doubles as the dither amount.
metalAngle: Direction of the band ramp, in degrees. Also rotates Smoke's warp and Heat's scrolling band.
tintColor: Colour applied with a colour burn rather than a multiply, so the highlights stay near white while the darks take the colour - which is what separates tinted metal from a merely coloured object. Alpha is the amount.
innerDistortion: Warp strength inside the shape. This one is multiplied by the field, so it is calm at the rim and strongest through the thick of the form - that contrast is the whole gem impression.
outerDistortion: Warp strength of the smoke outside the shape, which is not tied to the field.
innerGlow: Brightness of the material inside the shape. On Heat this is the heat of the body; on Smoke it is how strongly the plume shows through the silhouette.
outerGlow: Brightness of the halo outside the shape. Needs Spread to have room - the layer bounds expand to match, so a big halo costs padding.
smokeScale: Size of the smoke plume. Lower zooms out and, because the warp is damped where it would alias, also calms it.
smokeSpill: How far the plume is allowed from the shape. At zero it is confined to the falloff measured from the layer's own alpha, so the smoke pours off the form; at one it fills the layer's bounds, which is what the reference does because there the shader IS the whole frame. It always fades out before the padded edge either way.
smokeInner: Colour filling the shape behind the smoke.
heat1: First stop of the ramp. Low values of the field land here.
heatCount: How many stops of the ramp are used.
speed: Rate the pattern moves. Zero freezes it.
backColor: Colour behind the result. Transparent by default so it composites over whatever is beneath.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: A gradient blended from colour spots, warped by waves.

colorCount: How many stops are used. This is also the SPOT COUNT - each colour is one spot in the field.
positions: Slides every spot along its own path. A seed, not a count - changing it rearranges the composition without changing how many spots there are.
swirl: Twists the field about its centre, strongest there and falling away with distance. It breathes slowly rather than holding a fixed angle, so it never settles.
mixing: Does two things at once, which is why one slider covers the whole range: it sets the distance falloff exponent and how sharply the nearest spot wins. Low gives hard stripes, high a gradual blend.
waveX: Sine distortion across the field, strongest through the middle and calm at the border.
waveY: The same on the other axis.
waveYShift: Phase offset of the vertical wave.
grainMixer: Eats into each spot's reach, so the boundaries between colours break up rather than staying clean.
grainOverlay: Noise laid over the finished gradient.
rotation: Rotates the whole field, in degrees.
evolution: Drives everything that moves, in degrees. Keyframe it, or drive it with a Frame behaviour - the rate is yours rather than tied to the comp clock.
loop: Makes the field return exactly to its start, so it can be cycled with no visible seam.
cycles: How many full revolutions of Evolution before it repeats. At 2 the field comes home at Evolution 720, not 360 - so a higher count travels further through the noise and gives more variation before the repeat.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Repaint the image with brush, oil or watercolour marks.

style: Which painting model to use. These are alternative renderings, not layers - stack two Paint filters if you want both.
estimatorRadius: How far to look when working out which way the image runs. The most expensive control here.
estimatorTaps: Samples used for that estimate. Drop it if playback suffers.
threshold: How similar in tone a neighbour must be to steer the stroke. Low values keep strokes inside one area.
blurRadius: Smooths the direction field, so strokes follow broad structure rather than pixel noise.
strokeWidth: Pixels between those taps. Zero collapses the stroke to nothing.
fieldMode: What steers the strokes: the attached shader, the layer's own contours, or a blend.
flowMix: Balance between shader-driven and image-driven direction. Zero is all shader, one all image.
mapChannel: Which channel of the field shader to differentiate.
fieldStep: Spacing of the samples measuring the field's slope. Larger ignores fine detail.
intensity: How far pixels are displaced. Every pixel moves this same distance, which is the point.
smear: Extra blur along the stroke direction. This is what turns displacement into a visible mark.
bristle: Randomises stroke length per pixel, so the smear breaks into hairs.
perpendicular: Rotates the stroke direction ninety degrees.
washes: How many flat tones the image is reduced to.
washRadius: Size of the edge-preserving flatten that forms the washes.
washThreshold: How different a neighbour may be and still join the same wash.
transport: How far pigment is carried, in pixels. Zero leaves flat washes with wobbly edges.
edgeFlow: Smears colour along wash boundaries, which is what leaves watercolour's dark rim.
washFlow: Carries pigment up the brightness gradient, draining dark areas and pooling colour at the edge.
flowJitter: Randomises how far pigment travels. Even transport reads as a filter; irregular reads as water.
flowScale: Size of the jitter field, in pixels.
wetEdge: How far wash boundaries wander, as pigment creeping through damp paper.
edgeDarkening: Darkens where a wash ends, as watercolour dries.
granulation: Mottled density where pigment settles into the paper.
paperTexture: Paper tooth, and the stock showing through pale washes.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the painted result.
field: Shader whose slope sets the Oil stroke direction. Its Scale controls stroke size, its Evolution animates them.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Procedural paper: fibres, folds, crumple and blotches.

paperContrast: How deep the surface reads. This steepens the normal's own Z rather than remapping the output, so the shading stays physical at both ends instead of just gaining contrast.
roughness: Fine tooth. Indexed off screen pixels, not the pattern, so it stays a constant size however the layer is scaled - film grain rather than surface texture.
fibre: Curling strands in the stock. This is the ridge structure of a noise gradient, so it costs sixteen noise evaluations - by far the most expensive layer here. Leave it low unless the strands are the point.
crumples: Faceted foil-like buckling. Two cell fields multiplied, one sharp and one soft.
folds: Creases radiating from a few seed points. The field returns the vector to the nearest seed rather than a distance, so each crease perturbs the surface outward from its own origin - which is what makes them read as folds rather than as contour lines.
drops: Sparse flecks and inclusions in the stock.
seed: Changes the arrangement without changing the character.
shadowColor: Colour the surface falls to where it turns away from the light.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Photocopier toner: blown edges, dither, speckle and drum banding.

exposure: Lightens or darkens the whole page before the toner threshold, the way the copier's exposure dial does.
contrastAmount: How hard midtones are crushed toward black and white. Responds to detail rather than overall brightness.
blurRadius: Radius of the blurred reference, in pixels. Small values pick out fine detail; large values act on broad areas.
edgeBlowout: Toner piling up at boundaries: a dark halo inside an edge, a bright one outside.
threshold: Brightness at which toner stops being laid down. Lower for a lighter copy, higher for a heavier one.
softness: Width of the threshold. Zero is a hard lo-fi cut; raise it to keep some tone in the result.
dither: Pattern that breaks gradients into grain instead of banding. Ordered is the copier-like one; Random reads as a coarser, older machine.
ditherAmount: Strength of the dither. Too much reads as noise rather than toner.
speckle: Blotchy unevenness in the black, so coverage varies the way a tired cartridge does.
speckleScale: Size of the toner blotches. Small values give large soft patches.
banding: Faint horizontal streaks running across the page, as a worn drum produces. Zero by default.
bandingScale: How closely the streaks are spaced down the page.
paperAmount: Fibre grain in the paper, visible only where the paper shows. Zero leaves the stock clean.
paperScale: Size of the paper fibre. The grain is stretched, so it reads as fibre direction rather than plain noise.
paperFolds: Creases radiating from a few seed points, lighting the sheet the toner sits on. The field gives the vector to the nearest crease rather than a distance, so each one perturbs the surface outward from its own origin - which is what makes it read as a fold and not a contour line.
paperCrumples: Faceted buckling, from two jittered cell fields multiplied - one sharp, one soft.
paperFibre: Directional tooth in the stock, lit rather than merely tinted.
paperRelief_: How deep the sheet reads. Steepens the surface normal's own Z rather than remapping the result. Zero on Folds, Crumple and Fibre together switches the model off and costs nothing.
paperSeed: Changes the arrangement of folds and facets.
inkColor: Toner colour. Cyan for blueprint, a flat spot colour for riso.
paperColor: Stock colour. Slightly warm off-white by default.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the copied result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Convert between rectangular and polar coordinates.

mapping: Rect to Polar wraps rows into rings, with the top edge at the centre. Polar to Rect unwraps rings into rows.
interpolation: Blends the remapped coordinate against the original one. 0 is a passthrough.
centre: Offset of the polar origin from the layer centre, in pixels.
angleOffset: Rotates the angular axis, moving where the seam falls.
tileMode: What happens outside the source: Clamp holds the edge, Repeat wraps, Mirror folds.
amount: Amount
Mix back to the unfiltered input.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Separate into spot inks, screen them, and overprint on paper.

process: Biases mottle character and ink translucency to suit the printing process. Use the presets for the full look of each - this only nudges the residual difference at matched settings.
separation: How the image is split into plates. Ink Density solves how much of each ink reproduces the target and overprints them - right for photographs. Source Colour skips separation entirely: one plate, inked with whatever the artwork already is, so flat spot colours print exactly. Reach for it when a build comes out washed - a Riso reaches bright colours fine with a drum of that ink, but BUILDING one from blue plus yellow needs a little of each, and that means paper showing through.
inkCount: How many plates print, from one to four. Riso is a spot process - pick inks from its catalogue that match your artwork rather than treating these as CMYK. Green 00A95C, Fluorescent Pink FF48B0, Federal Blue 3D5588, Bright Red F15060, Yellow FFE800, Orange FF6C2F, Purple 765BA7, Teal 00838A.
flatten: Edge-preserving smooth of the source before separation, over this radius in pixels. On photographic sources it collapses noise so band edges land on real edges instead of scattering pixel to pixel. On FLAT artwork there is nothing to smooth, so it does one thing instead: an antialiased edge pixel is a blend of the two shapes either side and resembles neither, which separates to an ink mix matching nothing and prints as a hairline - this snaps it to the side it is closer to. Raise it until hairlines go.
levels: Quantises each plate's ink density to this many discrete steps. 0 is continuous tone.
levelBias: Gamma on density before quantising, so levels are not evenly spaced. 1.0 is even.
bandDither: Perturbs the quantisation threshold near a band edge, so banding breaks up only where it would otherwise show.
screenType: The geometry the ink is broken into. Flat prints solid density with no pattern at all, which is what a Riso does. Ink Grain is separate and applies to all of them - a dotted press is grainy too.
dotShape: The level sets of the dot. Elliptical is the one that matters on press: a round dot meets all four of its neighbours at once around seventy percent coverage, and the tone jumps there. An ellipse joins along its long axis first and the short axis later, so the same join is spread over two smaller steps.
screenStrength: How hard the screen bites. At 1 a dot is either fully there or fully absent, which is maximum contrast against the bare paper beside it - that is what makes dark dots read as heavy. Easing it back keeps the pattern's shape and position but closes the gap between dot and gap. Average density is untouched, so the tone does not shift; only the pattern's contrast does. At 0 it dissolves into flat tone.
inkGrain: Depth of riso's uneven ink transfer. Weighted by coverage, so blank paper stays clean and solids stay grainy - unlike film grain, which peaks at mid density and disappears at both ends because it models developed silver rather than ink laid on paper.
inkGrainScale: Size of that speckle. Larger values coarsen it.
frequency: Pitch of the halftone screen, in pixels per cell - so lower is a FINER screen. The slider range is a suggestion, not a limit: type past either end for a very fine litho screen or a very coarse newsprint one. Below about one pixel per cell the screen is finer than the image can sample and flattens to plain tone.
dotGain: MECHANICAL dot gain - ink physically spreading on press, so the dots grow or choke. The optical half of dot gain is Paper Scatter below; they are different effects and were previously conflated in this one control.
toneFloor: How dark the separation is allowed to read the artwork. Flat vector work is full of pure-zero channels, which read as needing infinite ink - so the solve spends all its density chasing a black no ink can reach, and every colour sharing that zero saturates at a full plate and prints IDENTICALLY. Raising this says nothing is darker than that, so distinct tones stay distinct. It costs absolute depth: blacks lighten. Raise it when shapes are crushing together, lower it when you need real blacks.
yuleNielsen: Optical dot gain: light enters the paper between the dots, scatters sideways and comes back out from under one, so a halftone always prints darker than its dot area suggests. This is the Yule-Nielsen n factor, a real measurable property of the stock - about 1.7 for coated, higher for uncoated where the fibres scatter further. 1 turns it off, which is the naive Murray-Davies mix.
ink1Color: Colour of the first plate. Match it to a colour in the artwork for spot printing, or use a process ink to build colours by overprinting.
ink1Angle: Screen angle for this plate, in degrees. Traditional presses use 15/45/75/105 so the four dot grids never line up and moire. It only does anything when a screen is in use - with Flat there is no grid to rotate.
ink1Coverage: How strongly plate 1 inks. 0 switches the plate off.
ink2Angle: Screen angle for this plate, in degrees. Traditional presses use 15/45/75/105 so the four dot grids never line up and moire. It only does anything when a screen is in use - with Flat there is no grid to rotate.
ink2Coverage: How strongly plate 2 inks. 0 switches the plate off.
ink3Angle: Screen angle for this plate, in degrees. Traditional presses use 15/45/75/105 so the four dot grids never line up and moire. It only does anything when a screen is in use - with Flat there is no grid to rotate.
ink3Coverage: How strongly plate 3 inks. 0 switches the plate off.
ink4Angle: Screen angle for this plate, in degrees. Traditional presses use 15/45/75/105 so the four dot grids never line up and moire. It only does anything when a screen is in use - with Flat there is no grid to rotate.
ink4Coverage: How strongly plate 4 inks. 0 switches the plate off.
inkOpacity: Translucency of all inks. Lower values build density more gradually where plates overlap - soy-based riso ink is quite translucent.
registrationError: How far each plate drifts out of register, in pixels. In Source Colour there is only one plate and nothing to misregister against, so it instead samples the ink colour offset from the coverage - a boundary picks up the colour from just across it, which is the fringe you actually see on a misregistered print.
edgeBreakup: How far the ink boundary wanders, in pixels. It works by wobbling the coordinate the coverage is read at, so solid areas are untouched - a flat lookup does not care where you sample it - and only the boundaries move. Each plate breaks up independently.
edgeBreakupScale: Size of that wander. Small values chew the edge finely; large ones make it undulate.
keyline: Paper left open along every edge in the artwork, in pixels, so shapes are separated by a fine white gap. Not the same as registration error: that drifts a plate one way, opening a gap on one side and an overlap on the other. This pulls every ink back from every edge evenly. It follows the artwork's boundaries rather than each ink's, so two shapes sharing a colour still get a line between them.
keylineThreshold: How much colour has to change before it counts as an edge. Flat artwork needs very little; raise it on photographic sources, where texture would otherwise draw keylines everywhere.
inkLoss: Patchy ink transfer - areas where the ink fails to take.
inkLossScale: Size of the patches where transfer fails, as a fraction of about 45 pixels. 0.05 is fine speckle; 1 drops patches tens of pixels across. Floored at a 6-pixel cell so the detail octave stays above the pixel grid - below that a noise lattice is aliased hash with a fixed visual frequency, and no amount of scaling or extra octaves changes how it looks.
mottle: Uneven ink laydown breaking up flat areas of density.
ghosting: A faint second impression offset from the first.
seed: Re-rolls the registration drift, speckle, and mottle.
boil: Re-prints the sheet every this many frames, so grain, ink loss, mottle, edge breakup and each plate's drift are all different on every new impression and perfectly still in between. That hold is what makes it read as hand-printed rather than as animated noise - 2 gives the classic on-twos chatter. Zero holds one impression forever.
time: Connected to the composition time. Only used to advance the boil.
paperColor: The stock the plates print onto.
paperGrain: Paper fibre structure. Textures the blank stock.
paperFolds: Creases radiating from a few seed points, lighting the sheet the ink sits on. The field gives the vector to the nearest crease rather than a distance, so each one perturbs the surface outward from its own origin - which is what makes it read as a fold and not a contour line.
paperCrumples: Faceted buckling, from two jittered cell fields multiplied - one sharp, one soft.
paperFibre: Directional tooth in the stock, lit rather than merely tinted.
paperRelief_: How deep the sheet reads. This steepens the surface normal's own Z rather than remapping the result, so the shading stays physical at both ends. Zero on Folds, Crumple and Fibre together switches the whole model off and costs nothing.
trueColour: Corrects the print's colour toward the artwork's, as a GAIN rather than a blend. The regional colour lands on the artwork's while every local deviation from it survives - so the multiply where inks overlap, the misregistration band and the grain all stay at full strength, even at 1. A separation reproduces colour through real inks, and flat artwork usually sits outside what those inks reach; this closes that gap without giving up the press.
paperTooth: Fibre texture that shows through where ink has already printed, darkest in the densest areas.
outputMode: What the filter produces: the full print on paper, ink printed over the source, ink alone on transparency, or a single plate proof.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the printed result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: A soft noisy ring of smoke.

radius: Where the ring sits, as a fraction of the short edge.
innerFade: Eats the ring from the inside, so the middle opens out instead of filling in.
detail: Angular frequency of the wisps - how many of them go round.
turbulence: A second, finer polar octave scrolling the other way, so the smoke churns rather than rotating as one piece.
color1: Colour where the noise is thin.
backColor: Colour behind the ring. Transparent by default.
evolution: Drives everything that moves, in degrees. Keyframe it, or drive it with a Frame behaviour - the rate is yours rather than tied to the comp clock.
loop: Makes the field return exactly to its start, so it can be cycled with no visible seam.
cycles: How many full revolutions of Evolution before it repeats. At 2 the field comes home at Evolution 720, not 360 - so a higher count travels further through the noise and gives more variation before the repeat.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Tape wander, creases, head-switching noise and chroma smear.

time: Driven by the composition time. Disconnect it to freeze the tape artefacts.
speed: How fast the tape artefacts move. Zero freezes them.
noiseDetail: Octaves of value noise. This is called six times per pixel and dominates the cost, so drop it if playback is slow.
format: Biases the noise floor and chroma bandwidth to match a tape format. S-VHS and Hi8 keep a sharper picture with less noise; Video8 sits close to VHS. Every other control keeps its own meaning - this only scales how much noise and chroma bleed they produce.
creaseAmount: Strength of the horizontal crease band that sweeps up the frame.
creaseFrequency: How many crease bands fit in the frame height.
creaseSpeed: How fast the crease travels. Negative reverses it.
creaseThreshold: How high the wave must peak before a crease appears. Lower makes creases more frequent and wider.
switchingHeight: Height of the head-switching band at the bottom of frame, as a fraction of the layer.
switchingShift: How far the picture is dragged inside that band.
jitter: Horizontal noise inside the head-switching band.
bloomAmount: Horizontal step between the seven smear taps.
bloomStrength: How much each smear tap adds.
greenLag: How far the green channel trails the red in the smear.
blueLag: How far the blue channel trails the red in the smear.
gain: Overall exposure after the bloom is added.
humAmount: Strength of the rolling AC brightness beat.
humSpeed: How fast the hum band rolls up the frame.
edgeColor: Colour shown where the tape wave pulls the picture off its own edge. The original used a flat dark grey.
dropout: Density of short dashes where the tape has shed oxide, scattered at random scanlines and x positions. Zero removes them.
dropoutLength: Length of each dropout dash, in pixels.
dropoutPolarity: Colour of the dashes: +1 white, -1 black, 0 a mix of both.
tracking: Strength of a band of badly degraded picture drifting up the frame, as when tracking is off. Zero removes it.
trackingHeight: Height of the tracking-loss band, as a fraction of the frame.
trackingSpeed: How fast the tracking-loss band drifts up the frame.
hiss: Fine luma noise over the whole frame, like tape hiss. Independent of Noise Detail.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the tape result.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Colour fields marbled by layered swirls.

shape: The base field the swirl acts on. It is nearly constant across the frame at this scale, so almost everything visible is generated BY the swirl rather than being this pattern bent - Checks and Stripes differ more in character than in shape.
shapeScale: Frequency of the base field. On Edge it inverts: 1 is a tight edge, 0 a very wide gradient.
proportion: Shifts the field toward one end of the colour ramp, so one colour takes more of the frame.
softness: 0 gives hard banded edges between colours, 1 a raw linear ramp. Anything between quantises the ramp and then softens each step.
distortion: A noise warp applied BEFORE the swirl - it seeds it. Direction comes from one noise field and magnitude from a second.
swirl: Strength of each swirl pass. Amplitude falls as one over the iteration number, a harmonic series.
swirlIterations: How many swirl passes run. Because the amplitudes are harmonic this increases the warp's STRENGTH as well as its detail, roughly as the log of the count. Note it breaks before the last one, matching upstream: 10 runs nine passes.
scale: Zoom. Larger values pull the field in.
rotation: Rotates the whole field, in degrees.
colorCount: How many stops of the ramp are used.
evolution: Drives everything that moves, in degrees. Keyframe it, or drive it with a Frame behaviour - the rate is yours rather than tied to the comp clock.
loop: Makes the field return exactly to its start, so it can be cycled with no visible seam.
cycles: How many full revolutions of Evolution before it repeats. At 2 the field comes home at Evolution 720, not 360 - so a higher count travels further through the noise and gives more variation before the repeat.

value.author: samMularczyk
value.layerInfo: Refraction through a moving water surface.

size: Size of the caustic cells. Smaller values give a bigger, slower pattern.
caustic: How far the caustic field pushes the picture. This is the fine, fast refraction.
waves: A slow, large-scale wave that both displaces the picture and warps the caustic field's own coordinates, so the cells ride the swell instead of sitting still under it.
layering: Adds a second, finer set of caustic octaves at a different time rate. Doubles the cost of the field, so leave it at zero when the extra depth is not needed.
highlights: Additive sparkle where the caustic peaks, keyed off the same field sample rather than a second one.
edges: What a tap finds outside the layer. Transparent is the honest answer - there is no picture out there - but refraction opens wedges of nothing at the border, and Clamp or Mirror fill them.
edgeTrim: Fold against a rect inset by this much. A layer's outermost pixels are antialiased, and reflecting those doubles them into a hard seam.
evolution: Drives everything that moves, in degrees. Keyframe it, or drive it with a Frame behaviour - the rate is yours rather than tied to the comp clock.
loop: Makes the field return exactly to its start, so it can be cycled with no visible seam.
cycles: How many full revolutions of Evolution before it repeats. At 2 the field comes home at Evolution 720, not 360 - so a higher count travels further through the noise and gives more variation before the repeat.
amount: Amount
Mix between the original layer and the result.
